Midterm Elections Live Updates: Democrats’ Sweeping Win Resets Power in Washington

Democrats flipped seven Senate seats and overcame the Republicans’ House redistricting effort to capture control of Congress. President Trump told The New York Times that he would accept the results.

Latest

Democrats woke up on Wednesday still celebrating their seismic triumph in the midterm elections, after voters gave them control of the Senate and the House in a blistering rebuke to President Trump. The rout, which has dramatically reset the balance of power in Washington, stretched from coast to coast as Democrats flipped seats that had spent decades in Republican hands.

Mr. Trump, who had made the midterms a referendum on himself, imploring voters to act as if he were on the ballot, told The New York Times in an interview that he was “absolutely willing to accept those results” and was prepared to work with Democrats.

Among the questions remaining as Wednesday dawned were how big the Democrats’ House majority would be, and whether the party could yet widen its lead in the Senate. Ballots were still being counted in Alaska’s contentious Senate race and in the unlikely battleground of Mississippi, where less than 50 votes separated the two candidates.

But a blue wave had already become a red wipeout: Democrats flipped Senate seats in Maine, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, North Carolina, South Carolina and even Texas, according to The Associated Press. Republicans had held the Senate seats in Texas and South Carolina for decades. The Kansas seat had been red for nearly a century.

Senator Susan Collins, a long-serving Maine Republican who had repeatedly foiled Democratic efforts to unseat her, conceded her race to the Democrat Troy Jackson.

In Texas, James Talarico, a state legislator who became a national fund-raising sensation, toppled Ken Paxton, the scandal-ridden Republican state attorney general whom Mr. Trump had elevated to the nomination.

In South Carolina, Dr. Annie Andrews prevailed over Senator Darline Graham, the sister of the late Senator Lindsey Graham. And Dr. Abdul El-Sayed won in Michigan, becoming the first Muslim elected to the Senate, even after his defeated primary rival endorsed the Republican nominee.

The scale of the Democratic victory was beginning to come into focus: The party’s margin in the overall national vote for House seats was expected to be about 13 percentage points, the largest for either party in a congressional election in at least a half-century, according to estimates by The New York Times. Democrats made extraordinary gains with young voters and Hispanic voters, and significant inroads with voters who didn’t attend college, according to Times Voter Trends.

The wins also thwarted the redistricting effort Republicans had undertaken in hopes of protecting their House majority. Democrats won districts in Florida that Republicans redrew, and flipped a North Carolina seat that was also part of the G.O.P. redistricting effort.

Here’s what else we’re covering:

  • Democratic landslide: The results revealed an unambiguous mandate from voters for a check on Mr. Trump, who has pushed the limits of his power, and imperiled whatever was left of his legislative agenda. He and his administration will face investigations that are expected to consume much of the next Congress. Read our key takeaways ›

  • A complicated landscape: More than 400 Times reporters, editors, data analysts, video journalists and photographers are covering the midterms, seeking to understand a large country with voters who are complicated — and sometimes contradictory. Read more ›

  • Statehouses: Democrats notched other firsts in governors’ races. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman to be elected governor in U.S. history. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa will be the first Democratic governor since 1990, ousting Gov. Greg Abbott, a three-term Republican. And Dr. Amy Acton became the first woman elected governor of Ohio.

  • G.O.P. bright spots: Republicans fended off a significant challenge in a Senate race in Florida, with Senator Ashley Moody defeating Angie Nixon, a progressive Democrat. Byron Donalds, a staunch Trump supporter, was elected Florida’s first Black governor, keeping the Republicans’ hold on that office.

  • Ballot measures: Voters across the country also weighed in on a range of statewide issues, including abortion, how future elections would be run and how their own votes would be counted. Read more ›

Speaker Mike Johnson told Republican staff on a call this morning that he will not run to lead the House G.O.P. conference in the minority, according to a person familiar with the comments, paving the way for new Republican leadership in the chamber after the party’s drubbing.

The S&P 500 surged higher as exchanges opened for trading. The S&P 500 is up 1.7 percent and the Nasdaq Composite has risen over 2 percent. For investors, more important than who won is that the uncertainty created by the election campaign is over. Even many of the big artificial intelligence companies that could now come under greater scrutiny have risen in early trading.

It looks like Elon Musk deleted his X post on Tuesday morning to “Vote red today!” The post is no longer apparent on his profile as of this morning, and Musk has a tendency to quietly delete social-media messages that don’t hold up well. Doing that would be a mild form of acknowledging the reality that many Americans did not, in fact, vote red. Musk spent nearly $500 million to boost Republicans during the midterms cycle.

For months, Republicans salivated and Democrats cowered at a giant G.O.P. spending advantage in almost every marquee race in the midterms.

And then in an instant, on one evening, it no longer mattered.

Much is made during campaigns about fund-raising totals and spending plans. This year, it’s not clear that the money did much good.

The much-vaunted Republican war chest crashed into a tsunami of grass-roots momentum as the votes were tallied, raising serious questions — yet again — about the true power of money in national politics.

Republicans outspent Democrats on ads in almost every competitive Senate race, according to the media-tracking firm AdImpact, spending about $250 million more on Senate races than Democrats did in the general elections.

In race after race, that advantage went poof

Ad spending for the general election in key Senate races

Democrats won almost all of those races, powered by a national backlash to President Trump’s war in Iran and naggingly high prices that seemed stronger than anything ads could overcome. Paid media succumbed to public opinion.

Rick Jackson, a wealthy health care entrepreneur who self-financed his campaign for governor of Georgia, outspent his Democratic opponent, Keisha Lance Bottoms, by a nearly four-to-one margin in general-election ads, according to AdImpact data. It didn’t matter. Ms. Bottoms prevailed.

Republicans, financed by the world’s richest person, Elon Musk, doubled the spending of Democrats in the Senate race in Texas. And yet James Talarico secured a victory.

Most of the 20 biggest donors in the country were Republicans. Democrats had no answer for Mr. Trump’s super PACs, which spent $384 million on their own advertising barrage.

And yet.

For decades, the basic logic of fund-raising and advertising has gone like this: Candidates raise as much money as possible, to spend as much as possible, to run as many poll-tested ads as possible, usually as late as possible. The idea is that these messages, delivered ad nauseam, should work with enough volume.

“There are some election years where just the conditions are middling, and then you know the electioneering can make the difference,” said Lynn Vavreck, a political scientist who has written extensively about the impact of advertising.

But in a terribly difficult economic environment like this one? “You’re not going to advertise your way out of that,” she said.

Money can make a bigger difference in state or local races, buying name identification or opening up lines of attacks on unknown candidates. But candidates at the national level are often well-defined already.

This is not the first time these questions have been raised. Hillary Clinton outraised and outspent Donald Trump in 2016. Michael R. Bloomberg spent over $1 billion of his own money in the national Democratic primary and drew few votes. Joseph R. Biden Jr. and Kamala Harris outraised Mr. Trump in those final months of 2024 — and didn’t win.

“You don’t want to think that if you raise more money, you will win,” Ms. Vavreck said. “It’s not a disadvantage, but it isn’t sufficient.”

The nation shifted towards Democrats by around 15 percentage points in this year’s midterm elections, with much larger swings occurring among subgroups where President Trump made substantial gains only two years ago, like Hispanic voters and voters under 30. Democrats won around 70 percent of the vote with both groups, a much larger advantage than they held with those groups in 2020 or 2024, according to Times Voter Trends.

Ty Masterson, the Republican hoping to flip the Kansas governorship, released a statement that stopped short of conceding but acknowledged a difficult night for Republicans. Masterson is trailing State Senator Cindy Holscher, a Democrat, by more than 5,500 votes, according to The A.P., which has not called the race.

“The first count does not seem to be going our way, but the margin is narrow enough that Kansas law calls for another look, and we’ll let that process finish,” said Masterson, the president of the Kansas Senate.

Stocks initially wobbled on Wednesday as the Democrats’ victory became clear but have since rallied, with major benchmarks across Europe rising. The S&P 500 is expected to start trading around 1 percent higher when U.S. exchanges open later this morning.

Even the big A.I. companies expected to come under pressure from potential regulation, or restraints to data center building, nudged higher in pre-market trading. SpaceX, Elon Musk’s A.I. venture, fell, pointing to the likely attention to come on Musk’s roles in politics, government and as a business leader.

It was a rough night for the Make America Healthy Again movement, as many candidates aligned with it lost. Zach Lahn — who received a $1 million donation from a PAC associated with the movement, and who appeared alongside Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. last week — was defeated in the Iowa governor’s race. Ken Paxton, who also tied himself to the movement, lost in the Texas Senate race.

Some pro-MAHA candidates pulled through, including Julia Letlow in Louisiana, who was elected to the Senate. Still, the mood among MAHA supporters was bleak. “MAHA moms stayed home and it could’ve swayed some of these races that were unbearably close,” Alex Voetberg, a podcast host and leading voice in the movement, posted on social media.

Some races are still too close to call, leaving some questions unanswered, including how big the Democrats’ House majority will be, and whether the party could further widen its new majority in the Senate. In the Senate, we’re still waiting on results from Mississippi and Alaska. So far, Democrats have gained 19 seats in the House, but several dozen races have not been called.

Times Voter Trends showed voters across the country and in key Senate races almost uniformly shifted to the left. The Democratic Party’s margin in the national House vote is expected to be about 13 percentage points, the largest for either party in a congressional election in at least a half-century, according to Times estimates. Estimates are based off data from the voter file, election-night precinct results and polling.

Voters across every age group shifted to the left, according to Times Voter Trends. Even voters over the age of 65, a reliably Republican group, shifted to the left this year. White voters without a college degree, another Republican stronghold, also shifted towards the Democrats this year.

Four states on Tuesday elected their first Black governors, a total that exceeds the cumulative number of Black governors ever elected before this year.

Before Tuesday, L. Douglas Wilder was elected in Virginia in 1989; Deval Patrick was chosen to lead Massachusetts in 2006; and Wes Moore was elected in Maryland in 2022, then re-elected on Tuesday.

Joining that list on a single Election Day came Black governors in Georgia, Florida, Wisconsin and Nevada.

In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms, a Democrat and the former mayor of Atlanta, was the first Black woman to be elected governor in the nation’s history.

She was joined by Representative Byron Donalds, a Republican, who will also lead another southern state, Florida. Wisconsin elected its first Black governor, David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive and a Democrat.

And in Nevada, Aaron Ford, a Democrat and the state’s attorney general, defeated Gov. Joe Lombardo after leaning into a campaign message centered on addressing high costs and his own upbringing in a struggling household.

Finally, in a first for an American territory, Stacey Plaskett, a Democrat and the current nonvoting delegate for the U.S. Virgin Islands, was also elected governor.

Ms. Bottoms galvanized the state’s Democratic voters by positioning herself as a bulwark against President Trump’s policies. She ran in a campaign that was closely coordinated with that of Jon Ossoff, the Democratic senator, who won his re-election campaign by nearly 20 percentage points.

Mr. Donalds is the first Black Republican to be elected governor. He focused many of his efforts throughout his campaign to win over the state’s Black voters, who typically back Democrats. Mr. Donalds, a dedicated Trump ally first elected to Congress in 2020, pledged to address high property taxes in Florida, as well as streamline government agencies and work to expand school choice in the state.

In Wisconsin, Mr. Crowley, a former member of the Wisconsin State Assembly, has carved a path as a centrist politician willing to work with Republicans. He focused his campaign on issues facing the state’s working class voters, including the high cost of living.

Julie Bosman, David Ovalle and Reis Thebault contributed reporting.

With Democrats having taken control of Congress, countries around the world are wondering what comes next for their relationships with the United States. Some students in Tokyo and Sydney expressed hope that the results would check President Trump’s power after two years of disruptive tariffs and a war with Iran, both of which have driven up inflation worldwide. Others questioned whether the results would spur Trump toward more aggressive actions abroad.

It could still be a long wait for a call in the Alaska Senate race, where about a quarter of the vote remains uncounted. Senator Dan S. Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, is slightly ahead of Mary Peltola in the reported vote, but that lead appears to be somewhat fragile.

Most of the Election Day vote has been reported, and although these ballots favored Mr. Sullivan, he is underperforming President Trump’s 2024 margins among Election Day voters. In the 27 districts that had finished tallying Election Day votes as of Wednesday at 5 a.m. Eastern, Mr. Sullivan was running behind Mr. Trump by an average of 12 percentage points.

The bulk of the remaining vote is expected to come from mail-in ballots, some of which were cast close to Election Day, and others of which were postmarked by Election Day and will be received in the days after. These are expected to lean toward Ms. Peltola. The deadline to count these votes, as well as provisional ballots, is Nov. 18.

It is an open question whether either candidate will cross the 50 percent threshold needed to win outright. If not, the race will go to ranked-choice tabulation, which will not begin until Nov. 18.

While The New York Times’s election forecast was leaning slightly toward Peltola when it was shut down in the early hours of Wednesday, there are various sources of uncertainty that could counterbalance her expected advantage in the late mail vote. Issues include how many ballots came from voters who did not rank additional candidates beyond their first choice, as well as the potentially confounding presence of Gerald L. Heikes and Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr.

Nevada’s attorney general, Aaron Ford, reclaimed the governor’s office in Nevada for Democrats, according to The Associated Press, giving his party new momentum in a swing state that had voted for President Trump in 2024.

Mr. Ford defeated the incumbent governor, Joe Lombardo, a Republican, in one of the nation’s tightest races.

Mr. Ford, who will be Nevada’s first Black governor, jumped into the race in mid-2025. He spent the entire campaign emphasizing rising costs and tying the sitting governor to the president’s least popular policies, blasting the “Lombardo-Trump economy” at every turn.

His dual focus on affordability and Mr. Trump will likely be seen as a playbook for Democrats looking to win purple states, and Mr. Ford’s allies hope that his success this year will set up the party for a pivotal presidential contest.

Mr. Lombardo, a relatively moderate former sheriff, had for months been favored to prevail. But as Mr. Trump’s waning popularity dragged down Republicans across the country in polling, analysts declared the Nevada race a tossup.

To hang on, Mr. Lombardo had aimed for a delicate balance, praising some of Mr. Trump’s policies without fully embracing the MAGA right. He attacked Mr. Ford as too liberal, comparing his policy goals to socialism, and accused him of politicizing his lawsuits on behalf of the state.

And Mr. Lombardo had tried to convince voters that his administration had made inroads in diversifying the state’s economy, curbing unemployment and securing new funding for schools.

But most Nevada voters were deeply unhappy with the status quo. They said they were struggling with housing prices and expensive gas, while unwanted data centers proliferated. In Las Vegas, a slowdown in tourism had generated a wave of negative headlines, and the powerful Culinary Union christened the period the “Trump slump.”

Mr. Ford leaned into his working-class upbringing, describing a childhood pocked with hunger and his role as a young single father reliant on social services to get by.

“This isn’t just a theme for me, y’all, it’s my life,” Mr. Ford told a crowded church in Las Vegas a few weeks before the election as he discussed his focus on affordability.

Mr. Ford, who is fluent in Spanish, also prioritized reaching out to Latino voters, who make up about 20 percent of Nevada’s electorate and helped Mr. Trump win the state in 2024.

During the campaign, Mr. Ford has pledged to repeal Nevada’s longstanding “right to work” law, which weakens organized labor by allowing workers to opt out of unions at unionized workplaces. He also railed against corporate homeownership and vowed to cancel millions of dollars in medical debt for the state’s lowest-income residents.

The first Muslim elected to the Senate in United States history stood on the stage early Wednesday in front of a Michigan flag and an American flag and introduced himself.

“My name,” he said, using the full, proper, guttural pronunciation, “is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed.”

Hot, sweaty and packed shoulder-to-shoulder into the main space at Democrats’ ticket-wide election night party in downtown Detroit, the crowd let loose a roar of applause.

“Thank you,” he said. “You took a chance on the unlikeliest of candidates.”

Mr. El-Sayed, a Michigan-born Rhodes scholar and former public health official in Detroit and Wayne County, was not just an anti-establishment economic populist winning on what proved to be a beyond-their-wildest-dreams night for Democrats. He was all of that and the son of Egyptian immigrants.

And he didn’t merely beat former Representative Mike Rogers. He won after prevailing in a contentious primary election against Representative Haley Stevens — and then shrugging off her 11th-hour endorsement of Mr. Rogers. He won, too, after a general election that was among the ugliest, most racist, most Islamophobic campaigns in the history of American politics, with President Trump again and again calling him “a jihadist” and Mr. Rogers and his supporters all but painting him as a terrorist.

“As I was campaigning, some of you would come up and ask, ‘How come you don’t hit back? How come you don’t call them racist or hateful?’” Mr. El-Sayed told the partyers during his victory speech an hour before The Associated Press made its official call. “They weren’t targeting me. They weren’t just attacking me. They were targeting and attacking you. They were targeting and attacking the very idea of America.”

Hours earlier, before even the first polls closed, Rasha Basha, 56, stood near the stage. She wore an American flag bandanna tied around her neck. Atop her head scarf was a blue cowboy hat with white letters spelling out “ABDUL.”

“He’s like my son,” she said. “He grew up with my kids.”

Dana Mosa-Basha, 31, had a matching cowboy hat and an American flag sash.

“He was one of the first people in our community that had a commencement speech at the University of Michigan,” she said. “Growing up, I mean, we would never have thought in a million years someone with his name six years after 9/11 would be the graduation speaker at one of the best universities in the country.”

“The last month — the bigotry, the hate — it actually reminded me a lot of the Sept. 11 attacks,” said Abe Basha, 37. “My name is Ibrahim, but I changed my name to Abe.”

Mr. El-Sayed’s election to the Senate “would be bigger than anything maybe we’ve ever experienced as Muslim Americans,” Mr. Basha said.

For months, polls had suggested it would happen. Still, the onslaught of insinuations and accusations, plus the recent soap opera of the decisions of Ms. Stevens, made the outcome feel uncertain.

On Tuesday night in a quiet, out-of-the-way corner, Mallory McMorrow, a state senator who ran against Ms. Stevens and Mr. El-Sayed in the primary, said in an interview that voters were “disgusted.”

“Mike Rogers’s message, if I could summarize it, was ‘Health care costs are too high, and that guy’s a Muslim,’” Ms. McMorrow said. “It’s going to backfire in a big way.”

Elsewhere as the evening progressed, Democratic Senate candidates kept winning. In North Carolina and Georgia and New Hampshire. In South Carolina and Texas and Kansas. In Iowa and Ohio and Minnesota and Maine.

In Michigan, which last elected a Republican to the Senate in 1994 but also was instrumental in sending Mr. Trump to the White House in 2016 and 2024, votes trickled in past midnight.

But at 1:29 a.m. Wednesday, to ecstatic chants and cheers, Mr. El-Sayed took the stage.

“All the kids who watched this last month, all the parents who struggled to explain why the president openly mocked someone for their name and how they pray, let them know tomorrow that the bad guys lost,” he said.

And then he named names.

Mike Rogers.

“Enjoy your retirement,” Mr. El-Sayed said. “You chose hate. And Michigan chose hope.”

Vice President JD Vance.

“There is this delicious irony in the fact that you’re constitutionally obligated to swear me in,” he said.

And President Trump, who had called him “Abdul Ramadan” and used his middle name as an epithet.

“I know you struggled with my name,” he said. “You can just go on and call me senator.”

Gov. Tina Kotek, one of the few endangered Democratic incumbents in a difficult year for Republicans, prevailed in her re-election bid, The Associated Press said, as she was powered in the end by a pro-Democratic environment in her blue state.

Ms. Kotek, who had been the longest-serving House speaker in Oregon history before winning the governorship four years ago, defeated State Senator Christine Drazan, the same Republican she beat in her first run for governor.

Ms. Kotek ran in 2022 pledging to reduce homelessness, expand access to addiction and mental health services, supercharge housing production and improve public schools. Progress on all of those issues has been far slower than promised.

In 2024, she faced an ethics controversy over her efforts to give her wife an expanded role in state government, prompting the departure of three top aides and forcing the governor to abandon her plans and apologize. A state ethics commission later dismissed complaints against her.

Liberal Democrats in Oregon have been frustrated by Ms. Kotek’s efforts to woo business leaders and work with Republicans. The state’s largest teachers union, a traditional source of Democratic support and get-out-the-vote efforts, opted not to endorse in the race.

Recent polls have shown Ms. Kotek’s dissatisfaction ratings rivaling those of President Trump.

Nebraska voters rejected two ballot measures that would have legalized online sports betting in the state. Gambling companies supporting the measures, including DraftKings and FanDuel, poured more than $20 million into the campaign, promising new tax revenue for property tax relief. Opponents, who raised just over $1 million, warned that online betting would threaten the integrity of college sports and fuel gambling addiction.

Arizona voters have approved a ballot measure barring transgender student athletes from participating on teams that match their gender identity, The Associated Press reported. The measure also requires transgender students to use only those restrooms and locker rooms that match their sex at birth.

Two traditionally stalwart Democratic groups returned to the party fold these midterms after a dalliance with the G.O.P. in 2024.

Counties with a Black majority had drifted a little more than a percentage point toward Trump two years ago. But when the dust settled this election night, those places moved nearly 16 percentage points toward Democratic Senate candidates. The Democrats ended up beating their Republican opponents by more than 50 percentage points in some counties.

Young voters also appear to have come back to the Democratic fold after some signs they were willing to vote Republican. After counties with large numbers of 18- to 34-year-olds swung more than seven percentage points to Trump in 2024, they swerved left by nearly 23 percentage points this year.

Democrats marched to a landslide victory in the midterm elections on Tuesday as voters across the country raged at President Trump’s party, dealing Republicans stunning defeats from the Deep South to the prairie lands.

For the first time in decades, Democrats won statewide in Texas, taking not just a Senate seat but also the governor’s mansion. They won a Senate seat in Kansas, which had not happened in nearly 100 years. They flipped a Senate seat in South Carolina, a state that had barely been on the battleground map. And they seized House seats in such deep-red territory that Democrats are on a glide path to their biggest congressional majority in years.

Economic anxieties at home and a war abroad proved to be a politically toxic combination for Mr. Trump and his party. Democrats were on track to win the national House popular vote by the largest margin in a half-century.

The results amounted to an unambiguous mandate from the public for a check on a president who has pushed the limits of his power, and they imperiled whatever was left of a legislative agenda for Mr. Trump. Now he and his administration will face investigations that are expected to consume much of the next Congress.

Here are eight takeaways from a brutal night for Republicans:

Democrats stormed to power in the Senate.

A pediatrician in South Carolina. A minister in Kansas. A seminarian in Texas. A Paralympic gold medalist in Iowa. A logger in Maine.

Democrats had flipped half a dozen Senate seats by the time the clock struck midnight, taking control of the chamber in a sweep that seemed unthinkable just a year ago.

Entering Tuesday, Democrats did not hold a single Senate seat in a state that Mr. Trump had won all three times he ran for president. By Wednesday, they had senators-elect in six of them — including five that the president won by double digits in 2024. Democrats will enter 2027 with at least 54 seats.

The rout meant that for the rest of Mr. Trump’s second term, none of his nominees — whether for the Supreme Court or top administration posts — will be confirmed without Democratic consent. And because senators serve for six years, the Democratic victories promise to remake the chamber’s complexion into the next presidency.

The Democrats who flipped seats included Dr. Annie Andrews in South Carolina, the Rev. Adam Hamilton in Kansas, James Talarico in Texas, Josh Turek in Iowa and Troy Jackson in Maine.

In North Carolina, Roy Cooper, a former governor, became the first Democrat to win a Senate race in the state since 2008. In Ohio, former Senator Sherrod Brown completed a comeback two years after being voted out.

The breadth of the Democratic victories suggested that the dire political climate for Republicans did more to power the opposition party’s successes than anything else.

Democrats are amassing a big House majority.

Democrats flipped House seats in rural North Carolina and central Kentucky, in the suburbs of St. Louis and Omaha, and all along the Texas border. They seized three seats in Iowa and four in Pennsylvania. They rebuffed redrawn lines in Florida.

It was a romp.

Democrats made inroads deep into Republican territory, prevailing in a Kentucky district, for instance, that Mr. Trump carried by 15 percentage points in 2024. But they also ousted some of the sturdiest Republican survivors, like Representative Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, who had been the lone House Republican to win election three times in a district that Mr. Trump lost three times.

Now Democrats are on track for a sizable House majority, with Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York poised to become the first Black speaker in American history.

Mr. Jeffries rushed to the rooftop of the Democratic Party headquarters in Washington on Tuesday night to film a video declaring that Republicans were “shook.”

The final size of the Democratic majority was still to be decided. But as of early Wednesday, Republicans had yet to win any of the most competitive races.

War, prices and an unpopular president cost the G.O.P.

“Pretend I am on the ballot,” the president said. His problem was that voters listened.

Before he lost the election, Mr. Trump lost the public’s trust on the issue that got him elected in the first place: the economy. And as the war in Iran dragged on, he struggled to defend a conflict that caused gas prices to rise, his MAGA coalition to fracture and Democrats to unite.

The president aggressively campaigned in the final month, jumping from one red state to another in hopes of reviving the energy of his flagging base. But the results showed the extent of the rebuke for Republicans.

In 2018 in Mr. Trump’s first midterm election, Republicans lost the House as suburban women revolted against his leadership. This time, the rejection seemed to come from virtually every corner of his coalition, including white working-class voters in places like Iowa, Ohio and Pennsylvania.

Mr. Trump, unsurprisingly, was defiant, distancing himself from his own defeat.

He began Tuesday morning by calling into Fox News to downplay the war in Iran. “When you talk about war, this isn’t really war,” he said.

He ended election night back on the phone with his favorite network that he sometimes loves to hate, speaking with the Fox News anchor Bret Baier.

“It’s just a point in time, Bret. Just a point in time. It’s the way it is,” Mr. Trump mused. “There was a mood in the air, I guess.”

Democrats scored seismic victories in Texas.

Democrats had dreamed for a generation of winning in Texas, one of the nation’s largest states, but they repeatedly fell short.

On Tuesday, they stormed to victory in the marquee statewide races. Mr. Talarico toppled Ken Paxton in the Senate contest, and Gina Hinojosa, a huge underdog, ousted Gov. Greg Abbott, a three-term incumbent.

Either outcome would have been momentous on its own. Both at once? That was more than Democrats could have hoped for not long ago.

At 37, Mr. Talarico is now one of the Democratic Party’s biggest stars. He overcame Mr. Trump’s attempt to cast him as outside the mainstream — “Talafreako” was the president’s derisive nickname — as well as the more than $200 million that Elon Musk spent trying to keep the state red.

“We just took back Texas,” Mr. Talarico told supporters in Austin.

At least some Hispanic voters in South Texas, a region that had swung toward Mr. Trump in 2024, swung back. Democrats claimed all four districts in Texas that border Mexico, which have some of the densest Latino populations anywhere in America.

“The nation will look at Texas and say we want something far more important than an election,” Ms. Hinojosa said in her victory speech. “They will look at Texas and say that faith in government has been restored.”

Republicans’ redistricting gambit sputtered.

In the summer of 2025, the White House pushed Republican state legislators to redraw their congressional lines to bolster the party’s chances of holding a majority.

The effort started in Texas and spread to North Carolina, Ohio and Florida. A Supreme Court ruling that dealt a new blow to the Voting Rights Act expanded the efforts to Alabama, Tennessee and Louisiana.

But the surge of Democratic voters on Tuesday overwhelmed some of the bespoke new G.O.P. seats.

The first Democratic House flip of the night came in North Carolina, a state that Republicans had remapped. Jamie Ager, a Democratic farmer, won a western North Carolina district that Mr. Trump had carried by 10 points. And the chairman of the House Republican campaign arm, Representative Richard Hudson of North Carolina, was in danger of losing his seat.

In Florida, Representatives Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz survived despite a new map that put them into more Republican territory.

In an interview, Mr. Jeffries praised House Democrats who ran in new, tougher terrain.

“So many of our colleagues made the patriotic and courageous decision to stay and fight,” Mr. Jeffries said, adding, “They didn’t run away from the fire. They ran toward the fire and helped put it out.”

He ticked eight of them off by name. As of early Wednesday, none of those lawmakers had lost, and at least six had won.

Governor’s races made history.

Democrats reclaimed a majority of the nation’s governor’s offices for the first time in two decades. They won at least five competitive races, in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, Texas and Wisconsin.

Voters also elected three new Black governors: a Republican, Byron Donalds, in Florida, and two Democrats, Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia and David Crowley in Wisconsin. Before Tuesday, only three Black governors had ever been elected in the country’s history.

Ms. Bottoms is the first female Black governor ever to be elected.

Ms. Hinojosa was the first Latina elected to lead Texas. Another Democrat, Xavier Becerra, was the first Latino elected governor of California. Deb Haaland, a Democrat, will be the nation’s first female Native American governor after winning in New Mexico.

There were other historic firsts, too.

Michigan elected the nation’s first Muslim senator, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat. New Hampshire elected a Democrat, Representative Chris Pappas, who will become the first openly gay man to serve in the Senate.

Peggy Flanagan, a Democrat from Minnesota, became the first Native American woman to win election to the Senate. A second Indigenous woman, the Democrat Mary Peltola, could join her if she is elected in Alaska.

Musk’s millions didn’t make a difference.

Mr. Musk, the world’s richest man, spent nearly half a billion dollars on the midterms. His party lost anyway.

Republicans, powered by Mr. Musk’s money and Mr. Trump’s $400 million super PAC, dominated Democrats in spending in this year’s Senate races. The Democrats still swept through the battlegrounds.

It was the second consecutive election in which the national party that spent more lost, after former Vice President Kamala Harris’s cash advantage was not enough in 2024.

Now Republicans face a daunting financial future. Democrats continue to dominate them at raising small-dollar donations online. And the lone Republican who has energized Republican small donors for the last decade is Mr. Trump. He will not be atop the ticket again.

Early in his term, Mr. Trump had suggested targeting some top Democratic donors for investigation, a move that seemed to put a chill on some contributors.

One of those whom the president had named, Reid Hoffman, the billionaire venture capitalist and LinkedIn co-founder, captured the Democratic Party’s emotions early on Tuesday evening with three emojis: “👀🇺🇸❤️”

With Democrats performing so well around the country, the party will be looking at Montana as a big potential missed opportunity. For months, supporters of Seth Bodnar, a well-funded left-leaning independent, and Alani Bankhead, the little-known Democratic nominee, feuded with each other and tried to pressure each other to drop out of the race. In the end, neither did and they split Democratic votes, helping Kurt Alme, the Republican, to an easy victory.

Dan S. Sullivan’s lead in Alaska’s Senate race masks the fact that he is underperforming President Trump’s margins in the 2024 race. Much of the reported vote is from ballots cast on Election Day, which are favorable for Republicans. In the 27 districts that have finished tallying such votes, Sullivan is running behind Trump by an average of 12 percentage points.

In District 22, which includes North Muldoon, one of the most diverse areas in the state, Mary Peltola, the Democratic candidate, leads by nearly 20 percentage points among Election Day voters. Trump carried the same district’s day-of vote by nearly four points in 2024. The remaining votes here will be from early and mail ballots, which are expected to lean toward Peltola.

Kurt Alme, a former federal prosecutor, won the Senate race in Montana, according to The Associated Press, allowing Republicans to hold on to an open seat in conservative territory. Alme, the former U.S. attorney for Montana, focused his campaign on reducing federal spending and bringing tax relief.

He entered the race in March after Senator Steve Daines withdrew his candidacy just minutes before the filing deadline. Daines and Gov. Greg Gianforte, a Republican, quickly endorsed Alme, as did President Trump. Some Democrats backed the independent bid of Seth Bodnar over their own nominee, Alani Bankhead, believing he was more electable in the heavily Republican state, and Alme was able to capitalize on the rift.

Representative Marcy Kaptur of Ohio, the longest-serving woman in Congress, defeated Derek Merrin, a Republican, according to The Associated Press, to win her 23rd term. Kaptur, 80, was first elected to the House in 1982. She edged out Merrin two years ago in an area that President Trump carried, and the Ninth Congressional District was redrawn to tilt more conservative. Kaptur prepared for the rematch by moderating her stances to defend her seat. She faced local Democratic backlash over an ad in which she said that “boys should not play in girls’ sports.”

Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive Democrat and outspoken critic of Israel, won Michigan’s Senate race, according to The Associated Press, maintaining his party’s hold on a crucial battleground seat despite a remarkable last-minute defection from his rival in the primary.

Dr. El-Sayed, 42, will become the nation’s first Muslim senator when he is seated in January. He defeated former Representative Mike Rogers, a Republican making his second run for the Senate, in a campaign that became one of the country’s most bitter and expensive contests.

Dr. El-Sayed overcame opposition not only from Republicans, but also, in the final days, from Representative Haley Stevens, the moderate Democrat he beat in the primary. On Sunday, after days of growing criticism of Dr. El-Sayed, she rescinded her support of the Democrat and made a stunning endorsement of Mr. Rogers.

Her late opposition was emblematic of a faction of moderate Democrats and Jewish voters who found Dr. El-Sayed’s position on Israel untenable. In the end, though, Ms. Stevens proved to have a limited constituency. Her endorsement of Mr. Rogers drew broad condemnation across the Democratic Party.

Dr. El-Sayed’s triumph gives Democrats a critical victory and keeps them in control of the seat held by Senator Gary Peters, who is retiring.

A talented orator and debater, Dr. El-Sayed ran on a platform of “money out of politics, money in your pocket, Medicare for all.” He focused relentlessly on tying Mr. Rogers to President Trump and his policies, especially the war in Iran and tariffs, which have driven up prices. He also reveled in schoolyard taunts, calling Mr. Rogers “a beta” during a Fox News appearance.

But throughout his campaign, questions lingered over whether he could win over crucial segments of Democrats’ traditional base. Black voters, especially in Detroit, have long had tensions with Arab Americans in the region.

And suburban Jewish voters who have been loyal Democrats for generations blanched at his suggestions that Israel should not exist as an explicitly Jewish state — a position he had softened by the end of his campaign — and that the United States should cut off military aid to the country.

In the campaign’s final weeks, Dr. El-Sayed faced a blitz of Republican attacks centered on his faith and family. At televised debates, Mr. Rogers questioned Dr. El-Sayed’s loyalty to America, invoked his mother and suggested he was in league with the Muslim Brotherhood, the Islamist political movement. (Dr. El-Sayed has disavowed the movement.)

Mr. Trump called Dr. El-Sayed a “jihadist” at a rally last month in Port Huron, Mich., and in Truth Social posts.

Throughout the campaign, Dr. El-Sayed emerged as a litmus test for Democrats. Progressives argued that his muscular left-wing politics were the party’s future and sought to cast his campaign as an example for others to follow. But centrist and moderate Democrats who backed Ms. Stevens in the primary saw his approach as an unnecessary risk in a battleground state.

Late in the race, a low-grade feud between Ms. Stevens and Dr. El-Sayed exploded into public view. Ms. Stevens had spent the campaign’s final weeks offering increasingly pointed criticism about Dr. El-Sayed’s position on Israel and demanding that he condemn an online ad made by an outside group that supported him. Dr. El-Sayed publicly uninvited Ms. Stevens from a planned joint appearance at a Detroit church; Ms. Stevens responded by pulling her endorsement and backing Mr. Rogers.

Dr. El-Sayed has telegraphed high ambitions in the Senate.

He has said he aims to influence Democratic policy on health care and Israel, both in Washington and during the 2028 presidential contest. Michigan is set to play a newly influential role in the party’s primary race, with the Democratic National Committee placing the state fifth on its revamped calendar.

Leading liberal figures flooded into the state to campaign for Dr. El-Sayed. Former President Barack Obama held a rally in Detroit for him, and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York accompanied him for a day of campaign stops. Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont held rallies to try to juice turnout for him.

The Senate race was the most expensive in state history, with $278 million spent on television and digital advertising, according to AdImpact, a media tracking firm. Dr. El-Sayed was outspent in both the Democratic primary, when pro-Israel super PACs supported Ms. Stevens, and during the general election against Mr. Rogers.

On the frigid evening of President Trump’s inauguration last year, after the vindicated president swept back into power and immediately pardoned nearly all of the Jan. 6 rioters, Representative Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York, gathered his top lieutenants for a quiet dinner in Washington.

In a private back room at Osteria Morini, an Italian restaurant on the Anacostia River, Mr. Jeffries, the relatively untested Democratic leader, and his team strategized for hours about how to use their limited power in the minority to check a newly empowered president who now had control of both houses of Congress.

Mr. Jeffries, according to a person who attended the dinner, was preoccupied with a single imperative.

“We just have to win,” he said firmly. “If we don’t win in 2026, it’s over.”

On Tuesday, Democrats did just that, claiming the House majority and putting Mr. Jeffries, 56, on the precipice of making history as the first Black speaker of the House. He presided over historic victories for his party that exceeded even their own expectations. Now, his actions will determine how effective Democrats can be in checking Mr. Trump’s power, and help set the agenda for the 2028 presidential campaign.

Here are five things to know about Mr. Jeffries.

He was raised in Brooklyn.

Mr. Jeffries grew up in a working-class home in the Crown Heights section of Brooklyn in the 1980s, when the now-gentrified neighborhood was a hotbed of Black activism but also overrun with crime and unrest associated with the crack cocaine epidemic.

The son of a social worker and a substance abuse counselor, who became a high-powered litigator, Mr. Jeffries grew up in a house that was described by longtime associates as teeming with Black nationalist ideas. His uncle, Leonard Jeffries, a professor at the City College of New York, was associated with the Afrocentrism movement and often expressed extreme views on the subject.

Mr. Jeffries and his brother, Hasan Kwame Jeffries, a history professor at Ohio State University, were pushed by their churchgoing parents to excel above all else.

“When Hakeem was growing up, Myrtle Avenue was known as Murder Avenue,” recalled Lupe Todd-Medina, one of his longtime political advisers. “It was not a place white people wanted to go. He grew up in this bubble of love, with lots of aunties around him. That also helped shape who he is.”

His mother and his aunt joined the Cornerstone Baptist Church, a Black house of worship, in the 1960s, and the congregation and its pastors became an important force in shaping Mr. Jeffries’s early life. Growing up, he served as an usher there. His grandmother predicted that he would one day become a pastor.

Mr. Jeffries has said that he has been motivated since entering law school by fights over racial justice. If all goes as expected and he is elected in January as the first Black speaker, he would be second in line to the presidency.

“That might be the thing that matters the most to him — breaking the glass,” Ms. Todd-Medina said.

At a victory party on Tuesday night, he ended his remarks with a note of hometown pride.

“We made it, Brooklyn,” he said. “We made it.”

He’s a moderate who was not Pelosi’s heir apparent.

Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi never exactly groomed her mentees, but she had a small circle of loyal House Democrats around her whom she viewed as potential successors. Mr. Jeffries was never one of them. But when he was elected by Democrats in 2018 to be the chairman of their caucus, essentially their chief messaging official and No. 5 leader, he was widely seen as having the potential to be the first Black speaker.

And four years later, when Ms. Pelosi acceded to calls to relinquish her role as the top Democrat, Mr. Jeffries quickly emerged as his colleagues’ top choice to take her place. He was elected House Democratic leader by acclamation after the 2022 midterm elections.

Still, while he is not expected to face a challenge for the job of speaker, Democrats are not unanimously thrilled about his elevation to become the most powerful man in Congress.

Though he is seen as a fresh face compared with the octogenarians who led Democrats in the House until recently, Mr. Jeffries is substantially more moderate than Ms. Pelosi and the progressives who are the largest bloc in the caucus. He is viewed as an establishment figure at a time when many Democratic voters are rejecting their party’s entrenched power structure.

He is cautious by nature.

Mr. Jeffries is known for his stentorian speeches and statements and his sharp-tongued attacks on Republicans. But he is a careful politician who avoids public confrontations and prefers lengthy private deliberation to quick moves. That has led some Democrats to view him as overly cautious, according to interviews with a half-dozen officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity to offer an unvarnished view of his standing.

They questioned whether he had the instincts to sustain the kind of fights that Democrats will need to show voters they can wage and win, now that they have swept into power in Washington.

Some House Democrats also said they had been surprised over the years when they did not hear much directly from Mr. Jeffries, even after successes or struggles. They had grown accustomed to Ms. Pelosi, who would constantly work the phones to keep her finger on the pulse of the caucus, often congratulating or commiserating with lawmakers as she quizzed them about what they were hearing. But Ms. Pelosi effectively operated as both the speaker and the whip.

These days, the duties are more divided, and it is Representative Katherine M. Clark of Massachusetts, the No. 2 who is in line to become the first female majority leader, who takes on the member management tasks that typically come with the job of chief vote counter.

Some of Mr. Jeffries’s allies said they expected him to act more aggressively and decisively in his new job.

“When you’re the speaker, you become the engine of the vote,” said Representative Gregory W. Meeks, Democrat of New York and one of Mr. Jeffries’s most trusted lieutenants. “Hakeem is ready to do just that. In the minority, your role is not as commanding.”

His pro-Israel stance has alienated the left.

Many democratic socialist candidates elected this year view Mr. Jeffries with particular aversion, regarding him as an establishment politician who has held back some of their progressive goals.

They also see him as too closely aligned with AIPAC, the pro-Israel lobbying group that has come to be seen by many Democrats as politically radioactive. The radio host Charlamagne Tha God has mocked him as “AIPAC Shakur.”

Mr. Jeffries bristles at the notion that he is beholden to any outside special interest group.

“Nobody can point to a single instance of me taking a vote that had anything to do with being influenced by any outside group,” he said in an interview earlier this year.

Still, Mr. Jeffries will face a major test next year from a progressive bloc of lawmakers who want Democrats to unite around ending military aid to Israel, which has bitterly divided the party. He will face competing pressure from more centrist Democrats, who have privately warned him that the party will get flattened if he goes too far in appeasing the left.

Mr. Jeffries is already cognizant of a need for Democrats to recalibrate their position on Israel. The question is how far he will be willing to go.

Earlier this year, he opposed a measure that nearly half of House Democrats backed that would have terminated U.S. aid to Israel. But in a letter announcing his position, he conceded that there were good reasons to back the measure and asserted that “a meaningful change in direction is needed” in the relationship between the United States and Israel.

He’s a Gen X leader who loves a hip-hop reference.

Mr. Jeffries, a Generation X leader in a Congress still filled with baby boomers, has made hip-hop culture a central part of his public persona, often peppering his speeches with rap lyrics.

During Mr. Trump’s 2020 impeachment trial, Mr. Jeffries ended his somber presentation with a lyric by the rapper and fellow Brooklynite Biggie Smalls: “And if you don’t know, now you know.”

At a news conference in February, he quoted the rapper Jay-Z while railing against redistricting in Texas.

“At what point will Republican extremists come to the conclusion that your reach ain’t long enough and your peeps ain’t strong enough?” he said.

He turned again to inspiration from Jay-Z in March, at a news conference related to the government shutdown.

“But for us, difficult takes a day, impossible takes a week,” Mr. Jeffries said, quoting a Jay-Z guest verse on Kanye West’s “Diamonds from Sierra Leone.”
content_text: Midterm Elections Live Updates: Democrats’ Sweeping Win Resets Power in Washington Democrats flipped seven Senate seats and overcame the Republicans’ House redistricting effort to capture control of Congress. President Trump told The New York Times that he would accept the results. Latest Democrats woke up on Wednesday still celebrating their seismic triumph in the midterm elections, after voters gave them control of the Senate and the House in a blistering rebuke to President Trump. The rout, which has dramatically reset the balance of power in Washington, stretched from coast to coast as Democrats flipped seats that had spent decades in Republican hands. Mr. Trump, who had made the midterms a referendum on himself, imploring voters to act as if he were on the ballot, told The New York Times in an interview that he was “absolutely willing to accept those results” and was prepared to work with Democrats. Among the questions remaining as Wednesday dawned were how big the Democrats’ House majority would be, and whether the party could yet widen its lead in the Senate. Ballots were still being counted in Alaska’s contentious Senate race and in the unlikely battleground of Mississippi, where less than 50 votes separated the two candidates. But a blue wave had already become a red wipeout: Democrats flipped Senate seats in Maine, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, North Carolina, South Carolina and even Texas, according to The Associated Press. Republicans had held the Senate seats in Texas and South Carolina for decades. The Kansas seat had been red for nearly a century. Senator Susan Collins, a long-serving Maine Republican who had repeatedly foiled Democratic efforts to unseat her, conceded her race to the Democrat Troy Jackson. In Texas, James Talarico, a state legislator who became a national fund-raising sensation, toppled Ken Paxton, the scandal-ridden Republican state attorney general whom Mr. Trump had elevated to the nomination. In South Carolina, Dr. Annie Andrews prevailed over Senator Darline Graham, the sister of the late Senator Lindsey Graham. And Dr. Abdul El-Sayed won in Michigan, becoming the first Muslim elected to the Senate, even after his defeated primary rival endorsed the Republican nominee. The scale of the Democratic victory was beginning to come into focus: The party’s margin in the overall national vote for House seats was expected to be about 13 percentage points, the largest for either party in a congressional election in at least a half-century, according to estimates by The New York Times. Democrats made extraordinary gains with young voters and Hispanic voters, and significant inroads with voters who didn’t attend college, according to Times Voter Trends. The wins also thwarted the redistricting effort Republicans had undertaken in hopes of protecting their House majority. Democrats won districts in Florida that Republicans redrew, and flipped a North Carolina seat that was also part of the G.O.P. redistricting effort. Here’s what else we’re covering: - Democratic landslide: The results revealed an unambiguous mandate from voters for a check on Mr. Trump, who has pushed the limits of his power, and imperiled whatever was left of his legislative agenda. He and his administration will face investigations that are expected to consume much of the next Congress. Read our key takeaways › - A complicated landscape: More than 400 Times reporters, editors, data analysts, video journalists and photographers are covering the midterms, seeking to understand a large country with voters who are complicated — and sometimes contradictory. Read more › - Statehouses: Democrats notched other firsts in governors’ races. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman to be elected governor in U.S. history. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa will be the first Democratic governor since 1990, ousting Gov. Greg Abbott, a three-term Republican. And Dr. Amy Acton became the first woman elected governor of Ohio. - G.O.P. bright spots: Republicans fended off a significant challenge in a Senate race in Florida, with Senator Ashley Moody defeating Angie Nixon, a progressive Democrat. Byron Donalds, a staunch Trump supporter, was elected Florida’s first Black governor, keeping the Republicans’ hold on that office. - Ballot measures: Voters across the country also weighed in on a range of statewide issues, including abortion, how future elections would be run and how their own votes would be counted. Read more › The S&P 500 surged higher as exchanges opened for trading. The S&P 500 is up 1.7 percent and the Nasdaq Composite has risen over 2 percent. For investors, more important than who won is that the uncertainty created by the election campaign is over. Even many of the big artificial intelligence companies that could now come under greater scrutiny have risen in early trading. S&P 500 - By Nate Cohn, Laura Bult, Nour Idriss, June Kim and Edward Vega - By Shane Goldmacher, Alexandra Ostasiewicz, Thomas Vollkommer and James Surdam - By Christine Zhang, Sutton Raphael, Brian Oh, Edward Vega and Stephanie Swart - By Shane Goldmacher, Alexandra Ostasiewicz, Jon Miller, Edward Vega and James Surdam - By Christine Zhang, Sutton Raphael, Brian Oh, Stephanie Swart and Edward Vega - By Evan Reynolds, Laura Bult, Nour Idriss, June Kim and Edward Vega - By Shane Goldmacher, Alexandra Ostasiewicz, Thomas Vollkommer, James Surdam and Edward Vega - By Christine Zhang, Sutton Raphael, Brian Oh and Stephanie Swart - By Evan Reynolds, Laura Bult, Nour Idriss, June Kim and Edward Vega It looks like Elon Musk deleted his X post on Tuesday morning to “Vote red today!” The post is no longer apparent on his profile as of this morning, and Musk has a tendency to quietly delete social-media messages that don’t hold up well. Doing that would be a mild form of acknowledging the reality that many Americans did not, in fact, vote red. Musk spent nearly $500 million to boost Republicans during the midterms cycle. For months, Republicans salivated and Democrats cowered at a giant G.O.P. spending advantage in almost every marquee race in the midterms. And then in an instant, on one evening, it no longer mattered. Much is made during campaigns about fund-raising totals and spending plans. This year, it’s not clear that the money did much good. The much-vaunted Republican war chest crashed into a tsunami of grass-roots momentum as the votes were tallied, raising serious questions — yet again — about the true power of money in national politics. Republicans outspent Democrats on ads in almost every competitive Senate race, according to the media-tracking firm AdImpact, spending about $250 million more on Senate races than Democrats did in the general elections. In race after race, that advantage went poof Ad spending for the general election in key Senate races Democrats won almost all of those races, powered by a national backlash to President Trump’s war in Iran and naggingly high prices that seemed stronger than anything ads could overcome. Paid media succumbed to public opinion. Rick Jackson, a wealthy health care entrepreneur who self-financed his campaign for governor of Georgia, outspent his Democratic opponent, Keisha Lance Bottoms, by a nearly four-to-one margin in general-election ads, according to AdImpact data. It didn’t matter. Ms. Bottoms prevailed. Republicans, financed by the world’s richest person, Elon Musk, doubled the spending of Democrats in the Senate race in Texas. And yet James Talarico secured a victory. Most of the 20 biggest donors in the country were Republicans. Democrats had no answer for Mr. Trump’s super PACs, which spent $384 million on their own advertising barrage. And yet. For decades, the basic logic of fund-raising and advertising has gone like this: Candidates raise as much money as possible, to spend as much as possible, to run as many poll-tested ads as possible, usually as late as possible. The idea is that these messages, delivered ad nauseam, should work with enough volume. “There are some election years where just the conditions are middling, and then you know the electioneering can make the difference,” said Lynn Vavreck, a political scientist who has written extensively about the impact of advertising. But in a terribly difficult economic environment like this one? “You’re not going to advertise your way out of that,” she said. Money can make a bigger difference in state or local races, buying name identification or opening up lines of attacks on unknown candidates. But candidates at the national level are often well-defined already. This is not the first time these questions have been raised. Hillary Clinton outraised and outspent Donald Trump in 2016. Michael R. Bloomberg spent over $1 billion of his own money in the national Democratic primary and drew few votes. Joseph R. Biden Jr. and Kamala Harris outraised Mr. Trump in those final months of 2024 — and didn’t win. “You don’t want to think that if you raise more money, you will win,” Ms. Vavreck said. “It’s not a disadvantage, but it isn’t sufficient.” The nation shifted towards Democrats by around 15 percentage points in this year’s midterm elections, with much larger swings occurring among subgroups where President Trump made substantial gains only two years ago, like Hispanic voters and voters under 30. Democrats won around 70 percent of the vote with both groups, a much larger advantage than they held with those groups in 2020 or 2024, according to Times Voter Trends. Ty Masterson, the Republican hoping to flip the Kansas governorship, released a statement that stopped short of conceding but acknowledged a difficult night for Republicans. Masterson is trailing State Senator Cindy Holscher, a Democrat, by more than 5,500 votes, according to The A.P., which has not called the race. “The first count does not seem to be going our way, but the margin is narrow enough that Kansas law calls for another look, and we’ll let that process finish,” said Masterson, the president of the Kansas Senate. Stocks initially wobbled on Wednesday as the Democrats’ victory became clear but have since rallied, with major benchmarks across Europe rising. The S&P 500 is expected to start trading around 1 percent higher when U.S. exchanges open later this morning. Even the big A.I. companies expected to come under pressure from potential regulation, or restraints to data center building, nudged higher in pre-market trading. SpaceX, Elon Musk’s A.I. venture, fell, pointing to the likely attention to come on Musk’s roles in politics, government and as a business leader. It was a rough night for the Make America Healthy Again movement, as many candidates aligned with it lost. Zach Lahn — who received a $1 million donation from a PAC associated with the movement, and who appeared alongside Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. last week — was defeated in the Iowa governor’s race. Ken Paxton, who also tied himself to the movement, lost in the Texas Senate race. Some pro-MAHA candidates pulled through, including Julia Letlow in Louisiana, who was elected to the Senate. Still, the mood among MAHA supporters was bleak. “MAHA moms stayed home and it could’ve swayed some of these races that were unbearably close,” Alex Voetberg, a podcast host and leading voice in the movement, posted on social media. Some races are still too close to call, leaving some questions unanswered, including how big the Democrats’ House majority will be, and whether the party could further widen its new majority in the Senate. In the Senate, we’re still waiting on results from Mississippi and Alaska. So far, Democrats have gained 19 seats in the House, but several dozen races have not been called. Times Voter Trends showed voters across the country and in key Senate races almost uniformly shifted to the left. The Democratic Party’s margin in the national House vote is expected to be about 13 percentage points, the largest for either party in a congressional election in at least a half-century, according to Times estimates. Estimates are based off data from the voter file, election-night precinct results and polling. Voters across every age group shifted to the left, according to Times Voter Trends. Even voters over the age of 65, a reliably Republican group, shifted to the left this year. White voters without a college degree, another Republican stronghold, also shifted towards the Democrats this year. Four states on Tuesday elected their first Black governors, a total that exceeds the cumulative number of Black governors ever elected before this year. Before Tuesday, L. Douglas Wilder was elected in Virginia in 1989; Deval Patrick was chosen to lead Massachusetts in 2006; and Wes Moore was elected in Maryland in 2022, then re-elected on Tuesday. Joining that list on a single Election Day came Black governors in Georgia, Florida, Wisconsin and Nevada. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms, a Democrat and the former mayor of Atlanta, was the first Black woman to be elected governor in the nation’s history. She was joined by Representative Byron Donalds, a Republican, who will also lead another southern state, Florida. Wisconsin elected its first Black governor, David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive and a Democrat. And in Nevada, Aaron Ford, a Democrat and the state’s attorney general, defeated Gov. Joe Lombardo after leaning into a campaign message centered on addressing high costs and his own upbringing in a struggling household. Finally, in a first for an American territory, Stacey Plaskett, a Democrat and the current nonvoting delegate for the U.S. Virgin Islands, was also elected governor. Ms. Bottoms galvanized the state’s Democratic voters by positioning herself as a bulwark against President Trump’s policies. She ran in a campaign that was closely coordinated with that of Jon Ossoff, the Democratic senator, who won his re-election campaign by nearly 20 percentage points. Mr. Donalds is the first Black Republican to be elected governor. He focused many of his efforts throughout his campaign to win over the state’s Black voters, who typically back Democrats. Mr. Donalds, a dedicated Trump ally first elected to Congress in 2020, pledged to address high property taxes in Florida, as well as streamline government agencies and work to expand school choice in the state. In Wisconsin, Mr. Crowley, a former member of the Wisconsin State Assembly, has carved a path as a centrist politician willing to work with Republicans. He focused his campaign on issues facing the state’s working class voters, including the high cost of living. Julie Bosman, David Ovalle and Reis Thebault contributed reporting. With Democrats having taken control of Congress, countries around the world are wondering what comes next for their relationships with the United States. Some students in Tokyo and Sydney expressed hope that the results would check President Trump’s power after two years of disruptive tariffs and a war with Iran, both of which have driven up inflation worldwide. Others questioned whether the results would spur Trump toward more aggressive actions abroad. It could still be a long wait for a call in the Alaska Senate race, where about a quarter of the vote remains uncounted. Senator Dan S. Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, is slightly ahead of Mary Peltola in the reported vote, but that lead appears to be somewhat fragile. Most of the Election Day vote has been reported, and although these ballots favored Mr. Sullivan, he is underperforming President Trump’s 2024 margins among Election Day voters. In the 27 districts that had finished tallying Election Day votes as of Wednesday at 5 a.m. Eastern, Mr. Sullivan was running behind Mr. Trump by an average of 12 percentage points. The bulk of the remaining vote is expected to come from mail-in ballots, some of which were cast close to Election Day, and others of which were postmarked by Election Day and will be received in the days after. These are expected to lean toward Ms. Peltola. The deadline to count these votes, as well as provisional ballots, is Nov. 18. It is an open question whether either candidate will cross the 50 percent threshold needed to win outright. If not, the race will go to ranked-choice tabulation, which will not begin until Nov. 18. While The New York Times’s election forecast was leaning slightly toward Peltola when it was shut down in the early hours of Wednesday, there are various sources of uncertainty that could counterbalance her expected advantage in the late mail vote. Issues include how many ballots came from voters who did not rank additional candidates beyond their first choice, as well as the potentially confounding presence of Gerald L. Heikes and Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr. Nevada’s attorney general, Aaron Ford, reclaimed the governor’s office in Nevada for Democrats, according to The Associated Press, giving his party new momentum in a swing state that had voted for President Trump in 2024. Mr. Ford defeated the incumbent governor, Joe Lombardo, a Republican, in one of the nation’s tightest races. Mr. Ford, who will be Nevada’s first Black governor, jumped into the race in mid-2025. He spent the entire campaign emphasizing rising costs and tying the sitting governor to the president’s least popular policies, blasting the “Lombardo-Trump economy” at every turn. His dual focus on affordability and Mr. Trump will likely be seen as a playbook for Democrats looking to win purple states, and Mr. Ford’s allies hope that his success this year will set up the party for a pivotal presidential contest. Mr. Lombardo, a relatively moderate former sheriff, had for months been favored to prevail.
